title: OpenAI bans Russian ChatGPT accounts tied to fake think tank influence op
subtitle: A covert campaign used ChatGPT to build a fictitious institute crediting Fukuyama and Chomsky, then piped its output to Substack, Telegram, X and LinkedIn.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI on August 25 disclosed and disrupted a covert Russian-linked influence campaign that had been using ChatGPT to manufacture the appearance of expert commentary. The operators worked in Russian and routed traffic through VPNs to defeat OpenAI's country block, then used the model to draft social media posts, translate them, and strip out linguistic tells before publishing to Substack, Telegram, X, Facebook and LinkedIn. OpenAI banned the account cluster and published a case study describing how it linked the activity.

The campaign centered on a fictitious 'International Burke Institute' — a website registered in February 2025 that falsely listed Francis Fukuyama, Noam Chomsky and other academics as affiliated experts. Of 36 articles OpenAI reviewed on the site, 34 had been copied wholesale from elsewhere on the internet. A signature deliverable was a 'sovereignty index' that ranked countries on a metric engineered to flatter Russia and criticize Western states. The value of ChatGPT to the operation was speed and polish, not novel argument: it collapsed the cost of producing plausible-looking English commentary at scale.

This is the seventh public influence-op takedown OpenAI has disclosed since it started reporting them in mid-2024, and it fits a well-established shape. State-linked operators aren't using frontier AI to invent new persuasion techniques; they're using it to industrialize old ones — fake experts, laundered talking points, cross-platform amplification. The disclosure lands as the EU AI Act's chatbot transparency requirements go live and as US lawmakers weigh a frontier AI oversight bill, both of which lean on the assumption that platforms will keep publishing what they find.

For learners: the defense against this kind of operation isn't a better detector — it's the same reading discipline that worked before generative AI existed. Check whether a source has a real institutional footprint. Search a paragraph verbatim to see if it appeared somewhere else first. Notice when a 'think tank' publishes only on aggregator platforms with no press coverage or citations. The mechanics of the Burke Institute are new; the tell — a website that looks credible but doesn't stand up to a five-minute source check — is not.
